> Cross-tracking: [GitCode #90](https://gitcode.com/openJiuwen/sciencediscovery/issues/90) (Chinese counterpart of this issue).

## What I was trying to do

Enter the app for the first time and figure out how to start my first analysis.

## What I saw instead

With no projects yet, the home screen shows a centered empty-state card listing three steps:

1. Configure a model (go to system settings → model registry, then save a provider token);
2. Create a project (its first session opens automatically);
3. Drop a CSV and ask (analyze the CSV and plot charts).

These are plain static list items (empty-state rendering in `apps/web/src/App.tsx`) with no click handlers: clicking "Configure a model" does nothing, and so does "Create a project". There is no composer, no upload area, no sample-data button, and no guided tour.

New users have no idea where to click; the three steps are signposts, but every one of them requires the user to find the destination on their own.

- Turn each step into a real action: "Configure a model" opens the matching settings section directly; "Create a project" opens the creation dialog directly.
- Add a prominent primary button "Load sample data and try it now": automatically create an initial project and session, load a bundled sample CSV, and prefill a ready-to-send example prompt, so a new user sees their first chart within seconds.

`katex` is still locked below the fix for CVE-2026-103923.

## Current pin

`apps/web` depends on `katex` `^0.16.47`. `pnpm-lock.yaml` resolves `katex@0.16.47`. The advisory is fixed in 0.18.2.

## What the advisory covers

From KaTeX 0.11.0 until 0.18.2, ordinary property access treats inherited properties on the renderer options, the trust setting, and namespace lookup as values the caller set. KaTeX does not itself pollute `Object.prototype`, and rendering an expression alone does not run script. If the prototype is already polluted, or an attacker controls the options object's prototype, a math expression can inherit a trust flag and emit links that a page then inserts.

## Expected

Depend on KaTeX 0.18.2 or newer.

issue:371.body:
`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` is still locked below the fix for CVE-2026-104850, and this repository uses the affected OAuth client.

## Current pin

`services/api` depends on `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` `^1.30.0`. `pnpm-lock.yaml` resolves `1.30.0`. The advisory is fixed in 1.31.0 on the 1.x line, and in `@modelcontextprotocol/client` 2.2.0 on the 2.x line.

## What the advisory covers

From 1.12.0 until those fix versions, the SDK's OAuth client lets the MCP server it is talking to choose which authorization server receives stored credentials. Stored credentials are not bound to the authorization server they belong to. A malicious or compromised MCP server can name its own authorization server in protected-resource metadata. Without another user step, the client can send that server the `refresh_token` and `client_secret` saved from an earlier sign-in.

## Why this tree is in scope

`services/api/src/mcp/oauth.ts` builds an `OAuthClientProvider` for custom MCP servers. The provider persists client information and bearer tokens, and it keeps a refresh token across token refreshes. That is the client shape the advisory describes.

## Expected

Upgrade `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` to 1.31.0 or newer and keep custom-MCP OAuth sign-in working. Until that upgrade, connect OAuth-enabled MCP clients only to servers the operator trusts.

## Source

https://gitcode.com/openJiuwen/sciencediscovery/issues/134

issue:376.body:
### Background

We want to automate the workflow from issue submission through code changes, review, and PR merge. This requires clear repository conventions so contributors and automation can determine whether an issue is ready for implementation, whether a change meets its acceptance criteria, and whether a PR is ready to merge.

The existing `CONTRIBUTING.md` covers development setup, test commands, E2E testing, and some PR requirements. Extend it with issue, commit, review, and merge conventions, supported by templates and checks that all contributors can use.

### Scope

#### 1. Issue requirements

Provide templates for feature requests, bug reports, and other supported issue types. Identify required and conditional fields:

- Background, the problem to solve, and the expected outcome.
- Functional specifications, including inputs, outputs, behavior, boundary conditions, and applicable compatibility requirements.
- Scope and explicit exclusions.
- Verifiable acceptance scenarios with preconditions, actions, and expected results. Cover success, failure, permissions, and recovery where relevant.
- Reproduction steps, environment, actual behavior, and expected behavior for bug reports.
- Dependencies, open questions, and blockers that must be resolved before implementation.

Include a complete example and define when an issue is ready for development. Clarify ambiguities that affect implementation or acceptance before work begins. Update the issue when the specification changes during implementation.

#### 2. Commit and PR requirements

Document branch, commit, and PR conventions:

- Follow the existing fork and target-branch workflow, and define naming and commit message formats.
- Link the PR to its issue and explain the reason, resulting behavior, and scope.
- Map each issue acceptance criterion to its implementation and validation result.
- Provide reproducible test commands, results, and supporting evidence. Distinguish tests that were not run, failed, were blocked, or were skipped.
- Describe compatibility impact, configuration changes, data migration, and rollback where applicable.
- Update affected documentation and follow the existing release label requirements.

#### 3. Review and merge requirements

Provide a shared review checklist and define:

- Checks for specification compliance, acceptance coverage, correctness, module boundaries, and applicable security and compatibility requirements.
- The distinction between blocking findings and suggestions, including how findings are resolved.
- Responsibilities for automated and human review, including approval authority.
- Which checks and approvals must be repeated after a PR changes.
- Conditions for entering the merge queue and completing the merge, consistent with the existing CI and `merge-gate` mechanism.

#### 4. Rule checks

Maintain a rule list that states applicability, verification method, execution stage, and failure handling for each rule. Include:

- Required issue and PR information and their linkage.
- Type checks, tests, user-perspective E2E testing, and documentation checks.
- License headers, sensitive information, temporary files, and generated files.
- Module dependency boundaries and compatibility requirements.
- Required checks, review decisions, and unresolved blockers.

Enforce rules through templates or CI where they can be checked programmatically. Provide explicit instructions for rules that require human judgment. Unavailable test prerequisites must be reported as blocked. Document the reason, approver, and follow-up for any exception.

### Deliverables

- Extend `CONTRIBUTING.md` as the common entry point, linking to separate documents where needed.
- Add issue templates, a PR template, and a review checklist.
- Provide a feature issue example and a corresponding PR acceptance report example.
- Map rules to automated checks, distinguishing existing checks, checks added in this work, and follow-up work.
- Resolve duplicated or conflicting guidance and identify where each rule is maintained.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Contributors can find issue, commit, PR, review, and merge requirements from one entry point.
- [ ] The feature template requires functional specifications and verifiable acceptance scenarios; the bug template requires reproduction details.
- [ ] The PR template requires an issue link, per-criterion acceptance results, and test evidence.
- [ ] The review checklist defines blocking findings, approval responsibilities, and re-review requirements.
- [ ] Merge conditions are consistent with the existing CI, merge queue, and `merge-gate` contract.
- [ ] Important rules specify applicability, verification, and failure or exception handling.
- [ ] At least one complete issue-to-PR example is included.
- [ ] New or changed templates and automated checks are validated, and documentation checks pass.

This issue covers the guidelines, templates, and agreed checks. Implementation of the complete automation system can be tracked separately.

issue:38.body:
> Cross-tracking: [GitCode #91](https://gitcode.com/openJiuwen/sciencediscovery/issues/91) (Chinese counterpart of this issue).

## What I was trying to do

Start the server and confirm "I can actually run analyses now".

## What I saw instead

- On Linux, when sandbox (bwrap) probing fails (e.g. the host disables unprivileged user namespaces), `services/launcher/src/preflight.ts` only prints a `WARNING` line; `services/launcher/src/serve.ts` ignores the result, keeps starting, and finally prints `ScienceDiscovery is ready at ...`.
- The green connection dot in the top bar only means the frontend can talk to the local API (`Connection OK`). It says nothing about sandbox availability, the scientific Python environment, or model quota.
- Users believe everything is ready, then the run fails mid-analysis — often with raw low-level errors.

## Why this is confusing

"Ready" and the green light create false confidence; the failure happens only after the user has invested time writing a prompt and uploading data.

## Suggested user-observable outcome

- When startup preflight finds the sandbox unusable, surface a prominent in-app notice ("analyses cannot run in this environment", with the reason) instead of a single terminal warning.
- Separate "frontend connected" from "compute ready" in the status indicator.
- Open question (needs a product decision): when compute is unavailable, should the app block new analyses entirely, or allow read-only browsing of past sessions and artifacts? The two strategies differ a lot in UX; decide before implementing.

Design note: the preflight result already exists in the startup chain (`runPreflight`); what is missing is exposing it to the web UI and layering the status display.

issue:385.body:
## Problem

Today a Specialist is a **role profile** (instructions + skills + connectors) injected into ScienceDiscovery’s native AgentLoop (`packages/schema/src/specialist.ts`, `docs/en/core/specialists.md`: *“A Specialist is not a new execution environment”*). Users can already `POST /api/specialists`, and `builtin-code-engineer` runs Python/R in the platform sandbox — but there is **no way to plug an external coding agent** (Codex SDK, Claude Agent SDK, iCode, Cursor SDK, OpenHands, …) in as the execution surface for a delegated `task`.

Users want to register custom specialists such as “code expert = Codex / Claude Code / iCode” and have the lead Agent collaborate with them on the same job (plan → `task` → artifacts → synthesize).

## Maintainer decisions (2026-10-18)

1. **Reuse the Specialist concept** — extend it; do not invent a parallel “External Agent” directory/API.
2. **Add a `runtime` field** when defining a Specialist:
   - `native` — current behavior (default when omitted).
   - **Known agents** — first-class SDK adapters, e.g. `codex`, `claude-agent`, `icode`, … (each with its own thin adapter).
   - **Unknown third parties** — `acp` (spawn command + argv; JSON-RPC/stdio per [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com/)).
3. Orchestration stays unified: lead Agent still uses `task(specialistId, …)` → independent Workspace / `inputPaths` / Brief / artifacts / `specialistConfigHash`. External runtime only replaces **who runs the model loop**.
4. Permissions: Always-allow is execution permission only; secrets still go through in-conversation config cards (#278: persist / this-run / alternate).
5. No platform-visible sub-`task` nesting; external agents may use their own internal subagents.

Related but **different** work: #64 is “ScienceDiscovery as an ACP **Agent**” (editors drive SD). This issue is “ScienceDiscovery as an ACP/SDK **Client/host**” (SD drives external coding agents via Specialist runtime). Share protocol knowledge; do not merge scopes.

## MVP decisions 2026-10-19 (Asia/Shanghai)

Locked by maintainer for the first Develop slice (do not implement full #385 in one PR). Full comment: see latest `repo-agent:status` MVP comment.

1. **Missing config**: Interactive config card so the user completes Codex auth/config in-conversation (do not wait for full #278).
2. **First SDK**: **Codex**.
3. **Process placement**: External runtime may run on **host** for MVP.
4. **Secret boundary**: Secrets **must not** enter specialist body / catalog argv; platform secret channel only.
5. **Usage**: Non-native allowed via explicit `task(specialistId=…)`.
6. **`specialistConfigHash`**: Only non-native `runtime` is hashed; native/omit keeps legacy hash.

### MVP acceptance (this slice)
- [ ] Schema/API optional `runtime` (default native) + `SpecialistRuntimeAdapter` + normalized event sink
- [ ] `task(specialistId)` non-native → Subagent/timeline/artifacts compatible
- [ ] Codex thin adapter end-to-end; code execution via platform channel
- [ ] Interactive config card for missing Codex config
- [ ] Hash policy (#6) + focused tests + minimal docs

### Out of MVP
UI runtime picker, ACP path, more SDKs, #64, full Skills/MCP bridge, full #278 product surface beyond the focused card.

## Proposed model (summary)

```text
SpecialistV2 = capabilities + role + runtime(native | sdk:<provider> | acp)
task(...) → SpecialistRuntimeAdapter.invoke(req, sink)
  → events: started | progress | tool_call | file_change | need_input | done
  → SpecialistResult (summary, artifacts, usage, runtimeSessionId)
```

Platform owns permissions, Workspace, artifact registration, audit. Adapter owns provider-specific session/stream/cancel.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Schema + API: `CreateSpecialist` / `Specialist` accept optional `runtime` (+ `capabilities`); omit → `native`; old clients unchanged.
- [ ] `SpecialistRuntimeAdapter` contract implemented for at least one known SDK (prefer iCode or Codex) and one `acp` third-party spawn path.
- [ ] `task(specialistId=…)` with non-native runtime creates a Subagent record, streams normalized events into the existing timeline, and returns compatible `subagent_result` / `artifacts[]`.
- [ ] Missing provider secrets emit `need_input` → #278-style config card; Always-allow does not skip secret provision.
- [ ] Probe fails → clear error + optional fallback guidance to `builtin-code-engineer` (no silent hang).
- [ ] Docs: user-facing “custom specialist runtime” + developer adapter guide; cross-link #64 / #278.
- [ ] Tests: adapter event mapping; cancel/timeout; artifact handoff; secret-not-persisted-in-specialist-body.

## Suggested milestones

1. Contract + native default path unchanged.
2. First known SDK adapter (iCode or Codex) end-to-end via `task`.
3. ACP fallback for unknown third-party commands.
4. Additional SDK adapters (Claude Agent, …) + UI runtime picker / probe.

## Non-goals (v1)

- Turning ScienceDiscovery into an editor ACP Agent (#64).
- Bridging all SD Skills/MCP into every external runtime (open follow-up).
- Multi-tenant sharing of `~/.codex` / `~/.claude` home state without isolation design.

## References

- Internal design draft discussed 2026-10-18 (Specialist dual-layer + adapters).
- Codex TS SDK, Claude Agent SDK, iCode `icode acp`, ACP, #278, #64.

issue:388.body:
## Summary

Complete model API compatibility across ScienceDiscovery by strengthening protocol tests, reusing the existing model adapters throughout the framework, and checking endpoint compatibility during configuration. This is an extension of existing support, not a new parallel model-client implementation.

## Current situation and problem

The main Agent model client already implements OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Messages. Swarm communicates with an internal Chat Completions gateway, which adapts requests to the configured upstream protocol. However, auxiliary paths such as Evolve, session naming and paper-related model calls still contain direct Chat Completions requests; inventory and verify their current behavior before changing them.

An endpoint or model name does not uniquely identify a protocol. Aggregators can expose several protocols, and apparent compatibility can conceal lost tool-call, stop-reason or reasoning state. Missing/malformed usage is a separate accounting problem and must not fail an otherwise successful task or prevent benchmark scoring. Existing usage work, including PR #304, should be reused rather than duplicated.

## Proposed scope

### 1. Strengthen UT/ST/Mock E2E coverage

Use deterministic local provider fixtures for all three supported protocol families. Cover request/history/system/tool translation; streaming text and fragmented tool arguments; tool IDs, parallel calls and result round-trips; required protocol-specific reasoning/signature state; completion versus truncation; cancellation, errors and malformed responses. Cover valid, missing and malformed usage separately, preserving unknown values rather than inventing zero usage or exact costs.

Include end-to-end mocked journeys through the Swarm gateway and affected auxiliary callers. These tests require no real model tokens. Newly added production code should in principle have 100% combined UT/ST coverage; document exact uncovered paths, reasons, risks and alternative verification. Passing Mock E2E is not UT/ST coverage proof.

### 2. Reuse existing adapters across framework callers

Inventory direct model HTTP calls, then route the in-scope Agent and auxiliary calls through the existing protocol-aware model boundary. Start with Evolve, session naming and paper-related calls, verifying actual capability and integration needs rather than blindly replacing URLs. Keep internal Chat Completions compatibility where components require it, with explicit upstream adaptation. Reuse Swarm/agent-core clients where applicable; avoid another provider router or duplicated protocol implementation.

Preserve system instructions, tool semantics, termination/truncation and error causes. Where a function genuinely cannot support a configured capability, surface a precise limitation; do not silently discard tools/parameters, change models or degrade to text-only execution.

### 3. Add configuration-time compatibility checks

For the supplied endpoint/model/credentials, expose an explicit compatibility-check action and detect which of the supported protocols work. Check actual response structure, not merely HTTP 200. Return per-protocol outcomes and independently report basic response, streaming, tool-call/result round-trip and usage availability. An endpoint may support multiple protocols; retain user selection/manual override and persist the chosen protocol rather than guessing each turn.

Use minimal bounded synthetic requests, timeouts and output limits; disclose that checks may consume paid tokens and obtain explicit user initiation/consent before requests. Separate confirmed incompatibility from authentication/authorization, rate limits, network failures and inconclusive responses. Nonstandard proxy prefixes and provider-specific headers must follow existing explicit configuration rather than guessed hostname/model rules. Recheck upon relevant endpoint/model/protocol configuration changes without silently starting chargeable probes.

## Acceptance criteria and boundaries

- Main Agent/Swarm and inventoried in-scope auxiliary callers use a shared, tested protocol adaptation path for Chat Completions, Responses and Messages; existing default configurations remain functional.
- Deterministic UT/ST/Mock journeys verify full tool-call round-trips, streaming, truncation and original error propagation, including auxiliary callers; no new paid real-LLM PR gate.
- Configuration checks show supported protocols and capability/unknown/error details; users can explicitly choose or override a result. No silent runtime protocol switching or fallback that could replay requests or corrupt history.
- Missing usage does not block Agent progress, success assertions or scoring. Usage unavailability remains visible for accounting.
- Probes, fixtures and logs redact credentials and do not send research task content; no secrets in URLs, public artifacts or browser persistence outside existing credential policy.
- Document supported protocols, configuration checks, costs, limitations and troubleshooting. Protocol compatibility does not certify the upstream model's identity, quality or routing, and cannot fix arbitrary supplier-side corruption.
- Gemini-native and Bedrock-native protocols are outside this initial scope. Automated probing does not guarantee compatibility with every nonconforming provider.

issue:392.body:
## Problem
The sandbox network consent card added in #381 (Fixes #324) offers **Allow once / Allow same type / Deny**. For a `sandbox_network` request the second button doesn't say what it covers. I checked on #381 head `fb2fe785`: choosing **Allow same type** for `eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov:443` does **not** widen to other hosts. A later request for `api.crossref.org:443` in the same run still raised its own card, because the resource is a per-host/run digest. Users can still reasonably read "same type" as "all sandbox network access", which is broader than what is actually granted.

## Expected
For `sandbox_network` cards, the user can tell exactly what each button grants. Either:
- rename the button for this action (e.g. "Allow these hosts for this conversation"), with a short scope hint, or
- hide it, if repeat consent for the exact same host set isn't a useful flow.

## Context
- Refs #381, #324.
- The button label comes from the shared key `permissions.allowMatching`, which every permission type uses. The fix should be action-specific, not a global rename.
- Repro: Ask approval mode → model calls `request_sandbox_network` for host A → **Allow same type** → model requests host B in the same run → a new card appears for B.

## Verification cases
1. **Label reads its real scope**
   - Preconditions: Ask approval mode; sandbox network `none`; the model calls `request_sandbox_network` with `hosts: ["eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov:443"]`.
   - Steps: Open the pending card in the conversation.
   - Expected: The card shows exactly one card for that host. The second button is either missing or its label names the host scope (not "Allow same type"). Allow once and Deny are unchanged.
2. **Grant never widens to another host (regression)**
   - Preconditions: As in 1.
   - Steps: Click the second button (whatever it is called) for `eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov:443`. In the same run the model then requests `api.crossref.org:443`.
   - Expected: A **new** card appears for `api.crossref.org:443`. The second host is not auto-allowed, and there are 2 `sandbox_network` permission requests in total.
3. **Other permission types unaffected**
   - Preconditions: Ask approval mode; the model calls `run_shell`.
   - Steps: Open the "Run a shell script" card.
   - Expected: Its buttons keep the current labels (Allow once / Allow same type / Deny) and behaviour.
4. **Global settings untouched**
   - Steps: Run case 2. Compare `GET /api/sandbox-network-settings` before and after.
   - Expected: The settings are identical.

issue:393.body:
## Problem
On #381 head `fb2fe785` (Fixes #324), in Ask mode with a domain-allowlist policy, resuming a blocked retrieval takes three cards in a row:
1. **Run a shell script** (approve the original `run_shell`)
2. **Sandbox network** for the observed denied host ("Continue the sandbox retrieval blocked by this execution")
3. **Run a shell script** again, for the NEW `run_shell` that carries `network_authorization_id`

Every step is correct by itself, but together they are heavy for a single user intent ("let this retrieval reach host X").

## Expected
One network decision is enough to resume. The re-run that consumes the one-use network token should not ask again for shell approval the user just gave, as long as it is the same kind of execution.

## Proposal / security considerations
- Reuse the prior shell approval only for the token re-run: same Session/Agent/run, same Runner, and the token is consumed exactly once.
- Do not carry the approval over if the command changes materially. At minimum, show the new command in the network card or require re-approval when it differs from the blocked execution. Otherwise a token re-run becomes a way to run unreviewed code with network access.
- Never inherit Always Allow / direct-execution consent; keep child Agents and later runs excluded, as #381 already does.
- Alternative: merge steps 2 and 3 into a single card ("Allow network to X and re-run this command").

## Context
Refs #381, #324. Observed in a local box run (API + bubblewrap runner + egress gateway, scripted model).

## Verification cases
1. **Baseline repro (current behaviour)**
   - Preconditions: Ask approval mode; sandbox network `domain-allowlist` with `allowedDomains: ["pypi.org"]`; the model calls `run_shell` with `curl -sS -m 8 -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' https://example.com/`.
   - Steps: Allow once on the shell card → allow once on the `example.com:443` network card → the model issues a NEW `run_shell` with the returned `network_authorization_id`.
   - Expected (today): A third "Run a shell script" card appears. After it is approved, the first execution has failed (`CONNECT tunnel failed`, HTTP 000) and the second has completed with HTTP 200 (2 executions in total).
2. **Same command, token re-run: single network decision**
   - Preconditions/Steps: As in 1.
   - Expected (after fix): Exactly 2 cards in total (shell, network). The token re-run with the identical command starts without another shell card and ends with HTTP 200.
3. **Different command must re-ask (security)**
   - Preconditions: As in 1, but the token re-run uses a different command (e.g. appends `; echo changed > marker.txt`).
   - Expected: A shell card is shown again, or the network card displays the new command before approval. It never runs silently.
4. **Token is one-use**
   - Steps: After case 2, the model calls `run_shell` a third time with the same `network_authorization_id`.
   - Expected: The call is rejected ("Unknown, consumed or foreign sandbox network authorization"), and no execution is started.
5. **No carry-over across scope**
   - Steps: Use the token or reused approval from (a) a child Agent, (b) a later run in the same Session, (c) another Runner.
   - Expected: Each is rejected or re-prompts, and no shell approval is reused.
6. **Deny path**
   - Steps: As in 1, but Deny the network card.
   - Expected: No re-run and no third card. The assistant reports the retrieval as blocked/incomplete, and the sandbox network settings are unchanged.

## Request

Integrate DeepSeek's official Search and Fetch APIs so ScienceDiscovery agents can search the web and retrieve page content from a specified URL through DeepSeek.

The providers listed in the current [Web tools documentation](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/main/docs/zh/reference/web-tools.md) do not yet include DeepSeek.

## Expected support

- Add DeepSeek to the Web provider settings, with API key configuration and an enable/disable option.
- Integrate Search via `POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search`, mapping titles, URLs, summaries, and other relevant results to the existing tool format for agents to use and cite.
- Integrate Fetch via `POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch`, returning the page title and Markdown content.
- Reuse the existing Web permission, credential protection, caching, and audit mechanisms. Document how the integration works with both the default JiuwenSwarm backend and the product's own Web tools.
- Provide clear errors for missing credentials, authentication failures, insufficient balance, rate limits, timeouts, and fetch failures. Handle empty search results through the existing fallback logic.

## Acceptance criteria

- After DeepSeek is configured, an agent can complete the workflow: search the web → fetch a result page → answer using its content.
- No DeepSeek requests are made when it is disabled, and existing provider behavior is unchanged.
- Add tests for successful requests, empty results, and major error cases, along with configuration examples.

Reference: [DeepSeek's official Search and Fetch documentation](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/zh-cn/guides/search/).

issue:398.body:
## Background

When running models on NPUs, the original task state cannot currently be recovered after a connection loss or error during execution. Users have to submit the task again, which may cause duplicate execution and unnecessary NPU resource usage, while making it difficult to continue tracking the original task's progress and results.

## Requested functionality

Support task state recovery after NPU model task disconnections or errors:

- Persist the task identifier, execution state, and available progress so the original task can be located after reconnection.
- For tasks still running on the backend, restore state synchronization, progress monitoring, and result retrieval without resubmitting the task.
- For completed tasks, recover and retrieve existing results without executing the task again.
- For tasks that have actually failed or stopped, show a clear error reason and recovery status. Allow execution to resume where recovery is supported, and clearly indicate when a fresh run is required.
- Prevent duplicate submissions during recovery or retries. If the original task's state is temporarily unknown, do not immediately create a new NPU task.

## Acceptance criteria

- After a connection loss during NPU task execution, reconnecting locates the original task and synchronizes its actual state.
- Recovery does not resubmit the same task when the original task is still running or has completed.
- After an error, users can see the failure reason and whether recovery is possible, and can resume the task when supported.
- After recovery, users can continue monitoring progress and retrieve results, reducing manual resubmissions.

---

## 需求背景

当前使用 NPU 运行模型时，任务执行过程中发生连接断开或错误后，无法恢复原任务状态。用户需要重新提交任务，可能导致重复执行、重复占用 NPU 资源，也难以继续跟踪原任务的进度和结果。

## 期望功能

增加 NPU 模型任务在断连或异常后的状态恢复能力：

- 保存任务标识、执行状态及已有进度，确保重新连接后可以关联原任务。
- 对于后端仍在运行的任务，恢复状态同步、进度查看和结果获取，无需重新提交。
- 对于已经完成的任务，能够恢复并获取已有结果，避免重复执行。
- 对于确实失败或中断的任务，展示明确的错误原因和可恢复状态；支持在具备恢复条件时继续执行，并明确提示必须重新运行的情况。
- 恢复或重试过程中避免重复提交同一任务；状态暂时无法确认时，不应直接创建新的 NPU 任务。

## 验收标准

- NPU 任务运行期间断开连接，重新连接后可以找回原任务并同步真实状态。
- 原任务仍在运行或已完成时，恢复操作不会再次提交相同任务。
- 任务异常后能够明确展示失败原因及是否可以恢复，支持在可恢复条件下继续任务。
- 恢复后能够继续查看进度并获取结果，减少用户手动重复提交任务的操作。

## What I was trying to do

Use the app full-screen on a 13–14" laptop, or in a side-by-side split (window width ≈ 900px, paper on one side, ScienceDiscovery on the other).

## What I saw instead

Instead of a collapsible drawer, the left sidebar (projects, sessions, search, system settings) turns into a full-width block occupying the top half of the viewport. The conversation is pushed to the very bottom and the composer is no longer in the middle of the first screen — you have to scroll to start typing (the composer bar is still visible at the bottom edge; it is not gone entirely).

*(A screenshot of the stacked layout at a ~900px viewport is available in the cross-tracked GitCode issue above.)*

## Why this is confusing

A new user opening the app in this viewport first looks for the input box, cannot find it in the visible area, and assumes the app has no input at all. It violates the common responsive-design rule that primary actions stay in the visible viewport.

## Suggested user-observable outcome

Below ~1024px width, collapse the sidebar into a drawer navigation by default so the central conversation area and composer always fit in the first screen.

Set the browser window (or DevTools viewport) to ~900px wide and observe the sidebar vs. conversation/composer layout.

issue:400.body:
## Summary

This issue is the delivery design for shipping ScienceDiscovery as a **desktop application on Windows and macOS**: one installer, one window, a first-run wizard, and automatic updates — with the code-execution and sandbox story settled per platform.

It is the design-level follow-up to #34 (desktop window) and #31 (Windows support), and it answers the questions those two left open: which shell framework, what to do about a Windows sandbox, how macOS gets a binary plus signing and notarization, and how updates reach installed apps. It also supplies the update mechanism asked for in #32.

## Where the product stands today

| Platform | Current state |
|---|---|
| Linux | Released binary and source mode; the UI is a browser tab on `127.0.0.1:4310`, reached with a bearer token. |
| macOS | Source mode only, officially supported on macOS 13+; sandbox is native (Seatbelt). No binary, no installer, no signing or notarization. |
| Windows | Not supported in any form. The existing `bubblewrap` + seccomp sandbox is Linux-only, and the runner, startup script, and binary packaging all assume a Linux or Darwin host. |

The practical effect: getting to a first screen means a terminal, a token copy-paste, and a browser tab, and a large group of researchers is excluded outright.

## Goals

- Download → install → wizard → working workspace, with no terminal, no token handling, and no manual environment setup.
- Windows covered without WSL being mandatory.
- Code execution stays inside the security contract the project already states, on both platforms.
- One shell codebase, one packaging pipeline, one release pipeline for both platforms.
- Installed apps keep themselves current.

## Non-goals for v1

- No Linux desktop build (Linux stays binary + browser).
- No forked frontend: the shell loads the same `apps/web` build against the same control API.
- No remote-execution provider on macOS. The remote link itself is cross-platform; only the Linux-hosted target ships with v1.
- No multi-instance support. Ports stay fixed and unique.
- No enterprise deployment formats (no Windows MSI, no macOS pkg).

## Root decisions

| Decision | Choice | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Shell | Electron, shared by both platforms | Same runtime family as the Node backend, identical rendering engine on every platform (the UI leans on Molstar, Plotly, Cytoscape), and the window, token injection, wizard, and orderly shutdown come for free. ~200 MB of memory is the accepted cost. |
| Execution environment | Windows: provider-based, direct execution by default, WSL and remote demoted to optional plugins. macOS: Seatbelt by default, fail-closed if unavailable, no remote. | On Windows the sandbox was always an interchangeable provider, so WSL becomes a plugin rather than the foundation — users who cannot install WSL are not shut out. On macOS the sandbox is already built into the OS and available on probe. |
| Bundling | Layered | Base package ~500–700 MB and works offline; large pieces (the WSL rootfs on Windows, heavy scientific dependencies) ship as on-demand plugin volumes; macOS ships per-architecture packages. |
| Architecture matrix | Windows: x64 only, tiered by OS version. macOS: 13+, arm64 as the mainline plus an x64 build. | Windows arm64 volumes do not justify the work yet, and direct execution has no hard WSL dependency, so older Windows versions remain covered. On macOS the conda scientific stack splits by architecture and a CPython/conda environment cannot be a universal binary. |
| Ordering | Windows is the first target platform, macOS the second. | Sharing the shell, packaging, and release pipeline costs the least when done once; macOS needs no backend adaptation and has a native sandbox, so it can reach internal beta sooner. |

## Execution model

### Shared

SD already models isolation as a replaceable enum — `bubblewrap` on Linux, `seatbelt` on macOS, chosen automatically by the backend. The desktop work adds a second, orthogonal question: **where** code runs.

### Windows: an execution-provider routing layer

- A routing layer above the existing sandbox enum answers "where does code run" with `windows-direct | wsl | remote`. The two layers stay independent: routing to WSL still isolates with bubblewrap inside it; routing to direct execution falls back to the approval mode because Windows has no OS-level sandbox. The existing enum does not change — new code is layered on top, so upstream merges continue to apply.
- **Capability probing, fail-closed.** The router assumes nothing about the machine: at startup it checks whether WSL is present, whether the private sandbox instance has been imported, and whether a remote host is configured. This reuses the existing sandbox-probe mechanism, caches the result for the session, and treats anything indeterminate as unavailable rather than routing on unknown state.
- **Hot switching.** Finishing a plugin install re-probes without restarting the backend. A persistent badge shows the active mode: sandboxed, direct, or remote.
- **Direct execution path.** The `run_shell` tool is bash-syntax and the model depends on it, so the bundled starter environment includes a bash compatibility layer (the MSYS2 port). Without it, direct execution could not run code at all.
- **Provider B (WSL plugin).** A trimmed, purpose-built Linux rootfs (~200 MB: bash, bubblewrap, system libraries, python3) imported under a dedicated instance name via `wsl --import`, bypassing the Store and its 1–2 GB download. Installation is a six-step state machine (detect → platform install → rootfs import → dependency check → network check → payload placement) with a journal after each step so an interrupted install resumes. A redistribution-compliance review of the Ubuntu base is required before this work starts; if it does not clear, the base moves to Debian.
- **No dead ends.** If the plugin cannot be installed, the user keeps direct execution, gets a specific failure reason with illustrated guidance, and has one-click rollback. Uninstalling the plugin deregisters the instance, clears the rootfs, and returns to direct execution with no residue.

### macOS: native sandbox, no routing layer

- macOS is a Unix platform; the backend stack already runs there in source mode, and Seatbelt is built in. The three heaviest pieces of the Windows plan — backend adaptation, the provider routing layer plus WSL plugin system, and the unsandboxed fallback — disappear or shrink sharply here.
- The default tier **is** the full sandbox. There are no plugins to install and no mode to switch; the mode badge stays visible and reads "sandboxed".
- If Seatbelt is unavailable (MDM-managed machines, nested sandboxing), the app fails closed with an explicit error and diagnostics. It does not degrade to unsandboxed execution the way Windows does.

## Packaging, signing, and distribution

| Area | Windows | macOS |
|---|---|---|
| Toolchain | electron-builder — one configuration produces both platform targets | same |
| Installer | NSIS, per-user install under `%LocalAppData%\Programs`, no UAC elevation anywhere | Standard DMG drag to `/Applications`; no permission special-casing |
| Artifact naming | `ScienceDiscovery-<version>-win-x64-setup.exe` | `ScienceDiscovery-<version>-mac-<arch>.dmg`, plus `.zip` as the update carrier and a per-arch `latest-mac.yml` |
| Signing | Current version is unsigned. The next version may add Azure Trusted Signing (OIDC short-lived credentials in CI, no certificate on disk). Identity validation is officially ~3–5 business days and can stretch to weeks if materials are bounced, so the application has to start early. | Public distribution requires Developer ID + notarization (notarytool) + stapling. Internal beta may ship ad-hoc with `xattr -cr` guidance, switching to the notarized chain as soon as it is ready. Apple account and certificate lead time applies. |
| Runtime pinning | — | The macOS build needs a pinned runtime manifest: CPython (both architectures), uv (mac wheel), micromamba (osx-arm64/osx-64), and the starter environment, all by version and hash. Today the manifest pins Linux only. |
| Distribution | All downloads are GitHub Releases assets. The website `/install` page is the primary entry point and the Releases page the secondary one; both link the same assets. No domestic object storage or custom domain. Plugin packages ship the same way. | `/install` shows two download cards and pre-selects the architecture by user agent, with manual override. |
| Updates | electron-updater reading Releases assets, stable channel only to start, `latest.yml` + blockmap for delta updates. | The zip is the update carrier: electron-updater downloads the notarized zip, replaces the `.app`, and restarts. The DMG is not part of the update flow. |
| Update-source stability | The update URL is fixed from the first public release, because installed apps have it baked in. | same |
| Interception | SmartScreen: unsigned cold starts are accepted for now, with documented "More info → Run anyway" guidance. | Gatekeeper: notarization plus stapling removes the prompt entirely; no user guidance is needed once that chain is live. |

## First run

- Three-step wizard: data directory → model configuration (preset provider → API key → live connectivity test) → done.
- On Windows the wizard goes through direct execution only: no environment preparation, no WSL involvement.
- On macOS the final step folds in the sandbox self-check. A failure shows a specific error page with diagnostics and a way to submit them, and **does not** let the user into the main UI. Ordinary users never see this page.
- Data directory defaults: Windows splits by provider — direct execution uses `%LocalAppData%`, WSL uses ext4 inside the instance for I/O performance — with a custom option and a free-space check. macOS uses `~/Library/Application Support/ScienceDiscovery` and offers a one-time migration when a source-mode `~/.sciencediscovery-data` is found.
- Model keys: Windows stores them with DPAPI, because `0600` file permissions mean nothing on NTFS. macOS keeps the existing AES-256-GCM + `0600` scheme.
- The access token is injected before the page loads; a token entry page appears only as a 401 fallback.
- Background work during first run (environment unpacking, stack start) reports real progress by file and byte count, with conservative time estimates, and gates the next step on a self-check.

## Security baseline

Shared:

- Workspace-directory allowlist; network calls require explicit authorization (egress denied by default, allowlist to permit, refusals recorded).
- A persistent badge in the UI states the execution mode.
- Supply chain: updates over HTTPS with integrity checks (sha512 in the Windows update manifest; same-chain signing and notarization for the macOS update zip). **Once signing is live, no unsigned version is published again**, and a signature-identity change is covered by a dual-identity transition window.

Windows direct execution (no sandbox):

- The permission mode is locked to "ask on dangerous operations" and the user cannot switch to "always allow". This is enforced server-side, so a modified frontend cannot bypass it. Usability is unaffected: safe operations never prompt, and dangerous-operation prompts offer "allow once" or "allow matching", so approving a class of operation stops repeated prompts.
- The stack is not multi-instance: fixed ports, loopback-only listeners; a port occupied by an unknown process is reported honestly rather than worked around.

## Compatibility

Windows:

| OS | Direct execution | WSL plugin |
|---|---|---|
| Windows 11 22H2+ | yes | yes (inbox component; mirrored networking available) |
| Windows 10 2004+ | yes | yes (`wsl --install --no-distribution`) |
| Windows 10 1909 and older | yes, degraded | no — explicit "not installable" message |

macOS: 13+ on arm64 (mainline — CI smoke and e2e run here) and 13+ on x64 (package plus lightweight validation); macOS 12 and older unsupported, matching the existing source-mode floor.

Known environmental constraints to handle explicitly:

- Windows path length (260 characters) versus deep Python package trees: guide toward a shallow data directory, keep the environment root shallow, truncate over-long filenames.
- Windows antivirus tools interrupting file writes during install and update, producing incomplete installs; unsigned builds add SmartScreen on top. Document allowlisting and maintain a known-issues library.
- Windows defaulting to GBK on Chinese systems: every script must specify UTF-8 explicitly.
- macOS App Translocation and the quarantine flag before notarization: both are resolved by signing, notarizing, and stapling.
- Missing Apple Silicon builds for a minority of packages: guide users to pip.

## Non-functional budgets

| Metric | Budget | Target |
|---|---|---|
| First run, fresh install to usable main UI | ≤1 min, both platforms | Windows ~30 s on SSD (environment ships in the package, so the cost is unpacking plus stack start); macOS near-instant |
| Packaged stack start | fast | port 4310 healthy within 30 s, both platforms |
| Minor-version update | delta only | Windows blockmap delta; macOS zip delta |
| WSL plugin install | real progress, conservative estimate | rootfs import plus dependency check within a fixed bound once the first release has data |

Memory: on Windows with the WSL plugin active, write `.wslconfig` limits (4 GB / 4 processors, adjustable in the wizard) so `vmmem` cannot take half the host. Direct execution has no `vmmem`. macOS needs no mechanism. The ~200 MB Electron shell is accepted on both.

## Process model

Three kinds of process, managed by one Electron main process:

| Process | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Electron main | Native window and OS integration (Windows: tray and system menu; macOS: application menu, Cmd+Q / Cmd+W); backend lifecycle (probe, start, clean shutdown); injects the access token before page load. |
| Renderer | The existing web UI; on first run it renders the bundled local wizard page first, then the main UI. |
| Backend stack | adapter (Python front door) + API (Node, business logic) + runner (code execution: the routing target on Windows, the sandbox execution point on macOS); memory-graph, evolve, and JiuwenSwarm start on demand. |

Startup: renderer wizard first (it needs no backend) → health probe every 3 s, reusing an already-healthy stack left over from a crash instead of starting a second one → otherwise start the stack → load the UI once the stack is healthy. Request path: page → adapter `:4310` → API `:4410` → runner `:4311`. Shutdown waits for running tasks, then stops only the children this process started; a reused stack is left alone. On Windows the window minimizes to the tray by default and closing it asks for confirmation when tasks are running; on macOS closing the window keeps the application and the backend alive, matching the backend semantics that a run continues after the page is closed.

Updates: checked at startup and every 6 hours; notify, download only on confirmation, never silently upgrade in the background. Installation first waits for running tasks and confirms all child processes have exited.

## Expected new components

- `client/shell/` — the Electron shell (shared; main process branches on platform, preload handles token injection and wizard IPC, `wizard.html` and `fallback.html` are platform-neutral).
- `packages/execution-router/` — the Windows execution-provider routing layer (no macOS counterpart).
- `packages/*/platform/` — per-package platform adapters (win32 and darwin side by side, single entry point, module boundaries enforced), e.g. a secret protector that uses DPAPI on Windows and AES-256-GCM + `0600` on macOS.
- `packages/sandbox-capability/` — extend the existing probe and runtime manifest with macOS entries.
- `scripts/start-stack.mjs` — packaged stack entry point, plus `stack-platform.mjs` for platform differences.
- `build/assemble-backend.mjs`, `build/resources/`, `build/rootfs/` — backend assembly (Windows x64 and per-arch macOS), the extraResources volume, and the trimmed WSL rootfs build (Windows only).
- `scripts/binary-release/runtimes.json` — add the darwin section.
- `.github/workflows/` — add Windows and `macos-14` (arm64) jobs for packaging (macOS including signing and notarization) and platform regression.

## Delivery milestones

| Milestone | Platform | Exit criteria |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | Windows | Download page → setup.exe → wizard → complete a small task with SD, never touching WSL. |
| M2 | Windows | On a machine without WSL: one-click sandbox install from the plugin center → run a sandboxed task → uninstall and fall back. |
| M3 | macOS | Source stack plus shell loading 4310 (backend ready, sandbox native — if the shell runs, this works). |
| M4 | macOS | Signed and notarized DMG, double-click to use: fresh Mac → download → drag install → wizard → complete a small task with no Gatekeeper prompt at any point. |

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Windows: a fresh machine installs and completes a task without WSL installed.
- [ ] Windows: the sandbox plugin installs in one click, resumes after interruption, and can be uninstalled cleanly.
- [ ] Windows: direct execution cannot be switched to "always allow", and the lock holds when the client is modified.
- [ ] macOS: a signed, notarized DMG opens with no Gatekeeper prompt and no `xattr` workaround.
- [ ] macOS: when Seatbelt is unavailable, startup fails closed with diagnostics instead of running unsandboxed.
- [ ] Both: first run reaches a usable UI within the stated budget on a fresh install.
- [ ] Both: an update lands as a delta, never silently, and never while a task is running.
- [ ] Both: the shell loads the existing `apps/web` build — no forked frontend.
- [ ] Both: quitting leaves no orphaned stack processes, and a reused stack is not stopped.

## Open questions

1. Is an Apple Developer identity available to the project for Developer ID signing and notarization? Public macOS distribution cannot ship without it, and the account lead time is real.
2. Do we start the Azure Trusted Signing application now so the next Windows version can be signed? If the answer is yes, the application has to begin ahead of the release.
3. When do we add a distribution path that is reliable from mainland China? GitHub asset downloads are workable but not dependable, and the update source is fixed once the first public release ships.
4. The shell is expected to live outside the main repository's git history. Is that acceptable to the maintainers, or should it live in-tree?
5. Telemetry is scoped to a minimal, in-app-disableable set with a published collection list (install success rate, first-run completion, Windows provider distribution and plugin install step outcomes, macOS architecture distribution, Seatbelt probe failure rate). Does that list pass review?

issue:401.body:
## Background

After a long-running tool execution fails, an Agent often has to infer completed work, reusable outputs, and possible continuation points from free-form logs. Execution state and logs alone do not provide a consistent basis for deciding where to continue.

Support recovery of failed long-running tasks: after the failure is addressed and the prerequisites are verified, the Agent can reuse completed results and continue from a supported recovery point, reducing unnecessary recomputation.

A shared, optional recovery metadata contract for tools and task adapters provides the supporting evidence. The LLM uses it to decide the next action; the framework persists and exposes it alongside the existing execution record, reusing existing execution tools and permission checks.

## Requested functionality

- Identify the original execution and expose completed stages or work units, the failed stage, and the failure reason when the task adapter can determine them.
- Reference reusable outputs and available task checkpoints using stable artifact/file/version identifiers where supported. Distinguish verified completed outputs from partial files.
- Explicitly report whether continuation is supported, unsupported, or unknown, including available continuation entry points and required inputs when supported.
- Describe conditions that must be checked before continuation, such as original execution termination, input/configuration changes, environment availability, and output validity.
- Preserve the metadata across refresh/reconnect and make it available through existing execution inspection and Agent tool results. Keep existing tools without recovery metadata compatible.
- Let the Agent inspect the evidence and choose repair, continuation, or a fresh attempt through existing execution tools and permission checks. Metadata itself must not automatically launch a replacement task.

The exact schema should follow the existing execution/tool-result architecture. Framework code should remain independent of specific scientific pipeline stages; task adapters supply domain-specific recovery information.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A shared, documented optional recovery metadata contract is available to long-running tools/task adapters.
- [ ] At least one supported long-running task adapter or representative test fixture demonstrates completed work, failed work, reusable result/checkpoint references, and continuation prerequisites.
- [ ] The Agent can retrieve persisted metadata after reconnecting and use it to identify a supported continuation point without relying solely on free-form logs.
- [ ] Unsupported or unknown recovery capability is explicit; the framework does not invent missing checkpoints or treat file existence alone as proof of completion.
- [ ] A running or unknown original execution is not automatically resubmitted because recovery metadata was returned.
- [ ] Tests cover supported/unsupported/unknown continuation, partial or invalid outputs, changed prerequisites, and persistence/readback.

## Scope and related work

- #398 covers reconnecting to the original NPU task, recovering its state/results, and avoiding duplicate submissions. This issue supplies structured evidence for Agent decisions after a confirmed failure.
- #278 covers in-conversation configuration and task continuation.
- This first version does not include arbitrary Agent-history rollback, restoration of process/NPU memory, or implementing model-specific computational checkpointing. Actual computational continuation depends on task-program support.
- Target release: **v0.3.0, October 30, 2026**, tracked in #249.

---

## 需求背景

长任务执行失败后，Agent 往往需要从自由文本日志中推断哪些工作已经完成、哪些结果可以复用、可以从哪里继续。仅有执行状态和日志，缺少统一的信息契约支撑这些判断。

支持长任务失败后的恢复：处理失败原因并确认接续前提后，Agent 能复用已完成结果，从受支持的恢复点继续，减少不必要的重复计算。

工具和任务适配器提供共享、可选的结构化恢复信息，作为上述能力的支撑。LLM 根据这些证据决定下一步；框架负责随现有执行记录持久化和提供查询，复用已有执行工具与权限检查。

## 期望功能

- 标识原执行；任务适配器能够确定时，返回已完成阶段或工作单元、失败阶段及失败原因。
- 通过受支持的稳定产物／文件／版本标识，引用可复用结果和任务检查点，区分已验证的完整结果与未完成文件。
- 明确返回可续跑、不支持续跑或能力未知；支持时给出可用续跑入口及所需输入。
- 描述接续前需要检查的条件，例如原执行已经结束、输入和配置变化、环境可用性及结果有效性。
- 刷新或重连后仍能通过现有执行查询和 Agent 工具结果获取这些信息；兼容不提供恢复信息的已有工具。
- Agent 根据证据选择修复、接续或重新执行，沿用现有执行工具及权限检查；返回恢复信息本身不自动启动替代任务。

具体字段设计应复用现有执行记录和工具结果架构。框架保持通用，由任务适配器提供具体业务阶段及恢复信息。

## 验收标准

- [ ] 提供有文档说明、可选的统一恢复信息契约，供长任务工具／适配器使用。
- [ ] 至少一个受支持的长任务适配器或有代表性的测试夹具，能够展示已完成工作、失败工作、可复用结果／检查点引用及接续前提。
- [ ] 重连后 Agent 能读取持久化信息，识别受支持的接续点，无须仅依赖自由文本日志推断。
- [ ] 不支持或能力未知时明确返回；框架不虚构检查点，也不把文件存在直接当作步骤已完成。
- [ ] 原执行仍在运行或结果未知时，不会因为返回恢复信息而自动重复提交。
- [ ] 测试覆盖支持／不支持／未知续跑能力、部分或无效结果、前提条件变化及持久化读取。

## 范围与关联

- #398 负责找回原 NPU 任务、恢复状态和结果、避免重复提交；本需求为确认失败后的 Agent 接续决策提供结构化证据。
- #278 负责对话内配置和任务接续。
- 首版不包含任意历史 Agent 状态回滚、进程／NPU 内存恢复，也不代替具体模型实现计算检查点。实际计算续跑依赖任务程序支持。
- 目标版本：**2026 年 10 月 30 日 v0.3.0**，在 #249 跟踪。

issue:405.body:
## Summary

Follow-up from [#276](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/issues/276) (closed). Recovery `direct_code` when sandbox is unavailable on local (#361) and reachable remote (#363) is done. This Issue tracks **agent-first direct execution**: the Agent may choose direct execution when the user asks to skip the sandbox (or the Agent judges sandbox unsuitable). The framework should **suggest** sandbox by default and keep the `direct_code` consent gate — not hard-require “sandbox already unavailable” before direct tools can be used.

## Background / decisions (from #276)

- Unreachable Runner / SSH repair: **out of scope** (user/network admin).
- Managed environment: **Agent decides**; ask the user when needed; **no** complex Settings for this.
- Architecture target recorded on #276: drop precondition `Runner reachable + sandbox unavailable` as the only path into `requirePrivilege({ action: "direct_code" })` → user allow → `run_direct_*`.

## Goal

Give the Agent policy control over sandbox vs direct; framework = suggestion + authorization, not a failure-only gate.

## Acceptance

1. Agent can initiate direct-execution consent while the sandbox is still available, when the user requested skip-sandbox or the Agent judges sandbox unsuitable (prompt/tool guidance makes sandbox the default preference).
2. Hard gate removed/replaced: reachable Runner (or local) still required; unreachable → clear failure + admin guidance; **no** requirement that sandbox be unavailable to *request* `direct_code`.
3. `direct_code` stays separate from sandbox `code` Always Allow (no silent carry-over); consent remains per command + scope + Agent run; no auto-replay / silent execute from chat text alone.
4. Sandbox tools and direct tools are peers; sandbox-failure errors may *suggest* direct but must not be the only way direct appears.
5. Tests/journey cover: user-predeclared direct while sandbox still “ready”; recovery path when sandbox unavailable still works; unreachable runner still blocked without SSH-maintenance feature.
6. Docs/prompt/tool copy updated for “prefer sandbox; direct needs explicit user consent.”

## Non-goals

- SSH maintenance for unreachable hosts
- Complex Settings for managed-environment presets
- Closing product gaps already accepted as out of scope on #276

## Related

- Parent: #276
- Delivered recovery: #361, #363

issue:41.body:
> Cross-tracking: [GitCode #94](https://gitcode.com/openJiuwen/sciencediscovery/issues/94) (Chinese counterpart of this issue).

## What I was trying to do

Click "+ Project", type a name (say, "Lung cancer differential expression analysis"), and start working.

## What I saw instead

Besides "Project name", the dialog spreads out the full runtime inheritance configuration:

- The title itself is jargon: "Project runtime settings — all settings are inherited by default; override only the fields that need different values";
- The task-model dropdown is full of technical markers: "Inherited · test · deepseek-v4-flash · ... (global settings)";
- Fields are annotated with "Effective source: global settings / built-in defaults";
- Optional extensions: "Connectors: inherited · 0 enabled";
- A Skills dropdown "Allow all skills";
- A skill-library radio card: "Select the libraries participating in M1 skill recall. Built-in skills optional, disabled by default. Head 8a87052b".

*(A screenshot of the current new-project dialog is available in the cross-tracked GitCode issue above.)*

## Why this is confusing

The user just wants a folder-like workspace but is forced to understand "configuration inheritance", "M1 skill recall", and "Git commit head" — implementation-level concepts rendered as-is into a dialog every new user passes through.

## Suggested user-observable outcome

- The creation dialog defaults to just "Project name" plus an optional "Research description"; clicking "Create" finishes the job.
- Model overrides, connectors, and skill libraries move into an "Advanced settings" section that is collapsed by default, keeping the same inheritance behavior as today (no change to effective values).

Design note: this only changes the default presentation layer of the form, not the backend inheritance semantics.

issue:413.body:
## Summary
Per [#323](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/issues/323) product decisions (2026-10-16): **Reviewer capability + automatic review should default on**; session Automatic review should be usable without a second setup step.

On current `main` (`a0cf9c7`, local source build, 2026-10-19), that is **not** what new / existing installs experience.

## Observed (local source `a0cf9c7`)
- Composer shows **Automatic review: Off** with status: `unavailable: Reviewer Specialist is off → Specialists`.
- System configuration → Specialists → **Reviewer** master switch is **off**.
- Built-in research specialists show 8/8 enabled; Reviewer is the gate that keeps auto-review unavailable.
- So “auto-review default on” cannot take effect: session auto is blocked by the system specialist default.

## Expected (from #323 accepted direction)
1. New installs / new sessions: automatic review effectively **on** without a second user trigger.
2. System Reviewer master switch must not silently block that UX — default it **on**, or remove it from the critical path.
3. Automatic review remains one-click off beside composer/session controls.

## Why a new issue
#323 is **closed** (completed) after PR work (#353 mentioned in-thread). The default-off Reviewer gate is still reproducible on tip `main`, so tracking a concrete remaining / regression gap separately.

## Environment
- Product: ScienceDiscovery local source mode
- Commit: `a0cf9c77c43ae046da078a398a9abc4420cf68b1`
- UI: English; Local Runner CONNECTED (`Version a0cf9c77 · local`)

## Acceptance
- [ ] Fresh data dir / new catalog: Reviewer Specialist defaults **on** (or auto-review runs without requiring that master switch).
- [ ] New session: Automatic review effectively on; composer does not show “unavailable: Reviewer Specialist is off”.
- [ ] User can still turn Automatic review off in one click; manual Run review still works.
- [ ] Docs/UI match the live switches (no reliance on deprecated `reviewMode` / `semanticReviewEnabled`).

Related: #323.

issue:414.body:
## Summary
**Functional bug:** Quick automatic review shows a full “passed” outcome after **citation-format / provenance checks only**, with empty findings and ~70ms runtime — no claim-fidelity check. Relative to [#323](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/issues/323) same-run review intent, this misrepresents verification depth.

## Repro context (shared)
- **Product:** ScienceDiscovery local source `main` @ `a0cf9c7`
- **Session id:** `a11aaecd-d8ef-4517-b6a8-7c1f22992c77` (local UI: http://127.0.0.1:4310/projects/39f9fe2c-a4c1-4911-9232-14de38dbfbd3/sessions/a11aaecd-d8ef-4517-b6a8-7c1f22992c77)
- **Artifact:** [`crispr-base-editing-scd-scan.md`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zy95-12/sciencediscovery/evidence/literature-scan-2026-10-19/crispr-base-editing-scd-scan.md)
- **Review JSON:** [`artifact-review.json`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zy95-12/sciencediscovery/evidence/literature-scan-2026-10-19/artifact-review.json)
- **Evidence screenshots:** [https://github.com/zy95-12/sciencediscovery/tree/evidence/literature-scan-2026-10-19](https://github.com/zy95-12/sciencediscovery/tree/evidence/literature-scan-2026-10-19)
- **Reviewer Specialist:** On · **Automatic review:** On · level **Quick**

### User prompt (exact)
```text
Do a brief literature scan on CRISPR base editing for sickle cell disease. Summarize 3–5 key recent findings with citations, then write a short markdown report artifact. Keep it focused.
```

![user prompt in timeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zy95-12/sciencediscovery/evidence/literature-scan-2026-10-19/01-user-prompt.png)

## What went wrong (locate here)
1. Open artifact after the run → Reviewer card says **Quick review passed**: “The applicable citation format and Artifact provenance checks passed.” Locked hash `b19742549423`.
2. Review record has `checks: [\"citation\"]`, `findings: []`, `decision: ACCEPT_AND_PROCEED`, `createdAt`→`finishedAt` ≈ **72ms**.

![Quick review passed — format/provenance only](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zy95-12/sciencediscovery/evidence/literature-scan-2026-10-19/02-review-passed.png)

![Automatic review still On](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zy95-12/sciencediscovery/evidence/literature-scan-2026-10-19/03-automatic-review-on.png)

```json
{
  "checks": ["citation"],
  "decision": "ACCEPT_AND_PROCEED",
  "findings": [],
  "reviewLevel": "quick",
  "createdAt": "2026-10-19T14:33:02.574Z",
  "finishedAt": "2026-10-19T14:33:02.646Z"
}
```

## Why this is a bug (not “effect”)
UI presents **PASSED** as if the report was substantively reviewed. Format-only ACCEPT with no “format-only / claim checks skipped” reason violates #323 acceptance (“explicit review outcome … or visible skip reason”).

## Expected
- Either run claim-fidelity checks in Quick, **or**
- Label outcome clearly as **format-only** / skip deeper checks with reason — never look like full verification.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Format-only Quick cannot display as undifferentiated “Quick review passed” for literature reports.
- [ ] Skip/partial reasons visible when claim checks do not run.
- [ ] Literature auto-review outcome distinguishes format vs claim-checked.

Related: #323, #413.

issue:42.body:
> Cross-tracking: [GitCode #95](https://gitcode.com/openJiuwen/sciencediscovery/issues/95) (Chinese counterpart of this issue).

## What I was trying to do

Let the agent run a data analysis, and when a permission approval pops up midway, understand it quickly and make a decision.

## What I saw instead

Under the default approval policy, when the agent prepares to run a Python script in the sandbox to analyze a CSV, the conversation pauses with a permission card: "[Code] Execute Python script", showing the code and three buttons: `Allow once`, `Always allow matching items`, `Deny`.

## Why this is confusing

- Nothing explains what "matching items" actually matches (the same script? the same tool call? scoped to this session or broader?), so users are afraid to click it.
- The user just asked "analyze my data" and is now asked for permission, which feels like something went wrong.
- Until a choice is made the analysis just sits there, and the card does not explain the "waiting" state.

Note: the composer area already offers an "always allow" switch — this issue is not about adding a master switch. The focus is the **wording of the approval card itself and the explanation of the matching scope**.

## Suggested user-observable outcome

- The card states each option's exact effect and scope in one sentence (e.g. "Allow once" lets only this call through; "Always allow matching items" stops asking for which calls within which scope — copy must match the actual behavior).
- The consequence of "Deny" is spelled out (the operation is skipped and the agent receives the denial).

Design note: first pin down the precise semantics of the three options in the current approval model, then write the card copy to match; a shortcut on the card to flip "always allow" can be evaluated as a follow-up enhancement.

issue:420.body:
## Problem and user outcome

Researchers need to retrieve domain-specific scientific data through MCP and use it in traceable ScienceDiscovery workflows. Literature search alone does not satisfy this need: the objects are expression datasets, bioactivity measurements, variant assertions, and protein structures.

Provide supported, discoverable connections to **GEO, ChEMBL, ClinVar, RCSB PDB, and AlphaFold Protein Structure Database**, with reliable retrieval, explicit data boundaries, and provenance that survives downstream analysis.

## Context and existing implementation

Request inspired by this article: https://x.com/servasyy_ai/article/2112052770287284550
Related project documentation: https://aipoch.com/docs/guides/connectors/

Source inspection of ScienceDiscovery at baseline `0d31e155` found existing MCP implementations for GEO, ChEMBL, ClinVar, and PDB in `services/gateway/src/sciencediscovery_gateway/public_biomed_mcp.py`, plus manifests in `packages/mcp-sources/src/public-biomed.ts`. UniProt, Ensembl, and Reactome provide additional reusable patterns. No built-in AlphaFold DB adapter was found in that inspection.

This is a request to complete and validate domain database support, reusing existing adapters. It does not assume these databases are entirely unsupported. The baseline assessment was static inspection, not a live end-to-end availability test; recheck the target version before implementation.

## Requested scope

| Database | Required user-facing capabilities | Domain details to preserve |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GEO | Search studies, retrieve study/sample metadata, discover actual processed/supplementary files, and download selected analysis-ready data | GSE/GSM/GPL identifiers, organism, sample conditions, platform, and whether data are raw counts, normalized values, or other processed data |
| ChEMBL | Search molecules/targets, retrieve bioactivity measurements with useful filters, and perform similarity searches | Molecule/target/assay IDs, assay type, organism, relation, value, units, confidence, and source references |
| ClinVar | Search/lookup variants and retrieve individual clinical assertions | VCV/RCV/SCV identifiers where applicable, assembly, condition, review status, dates, and conflicting submissions |
| RCSB PDB | Search/lookup experimental structures and download supported structure files | PDB ID, experimental method, resolution where applicable, chains/entities, ligands, and source/version metadata |
| AlphaFold DB | Retrieve available predictions by protein accession and download model/confidence files when available | UniProt accession, model identifier/version, source URLs, and confidence information |

AlphaFold DB retrieval is separate from running AlphaFold prediction software. New prediction compute infrastructure is outside this request. PubMed and other literature databases are also outside this scope.

## Integration requirements

- Reuse the MCP client, connector selection, permission/audit, and artifact download mechanisms. Prefer official provider APIs behind MCP adapters; do not require providers to expose MCP themselves.
- Make supported sources and operations discoverable, with setup instructions and any credential requirements. Enable the source for the intended Session and support both Inspector validation and Agent use.
- Return structured domain data and standard evidence records with stable identifiers, source links, retrieval time, and provider version/release when available. Retain source caveats and attribution.
- A generic custom MCP connection currently preserves raw/structured content but produces empty standardized `records`; calling a tool successfully alone must not count as complete evidence integration.
- Transfer large datasets and structure files through governed artifact jobs, with source metadata and integrity checks. Keep file bytes out of model context and distinguish a proposed download from a completed, verified artifact.
- Handle pagination, provider rate limits, timeouts, invalid identifiers, missing records/files, and partial failures explicitly. Do not silently present a capped subset as the complete dataset.
- Document scientific limits: GEO standard matrix/SOFT candidate paths do not enumerate all supplementary files; not every expression matrix is suitable for count-based analysis; ClinVar submissions can conflict; experimental and predicted structures must remain distinguishable.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On the target version, document the existing capability and remaining gap for each of the five databases.
- [ ] All five sources can be configured/enabled and successfully called from the intended Session; tool inputs and results are inspectable and audited.
- [ ] Each database has a representative live provider validation with recorded identifiers, commands/steps, expected results, and actual results. Record unavailable-provider cases as blocked rather than passed.
- [ ] GEO: discover actual files for a public study, retrieve relevant sample annotations, and download/verify a real selected matrix. Validate its data type and dimensions before downstream analysis; report when count-based analysis is inappropriate.
- [ ] ChEMBL: retrieve a target/molecule-linked activity set with explicit assay/measurement constraints, preserving units and relations, and verify pagination or clearly disclosed limits.
- [ ] ClinVar: retrieve assertions and preserve conflicting classifications/review status without reducing them to one unsupported consensus.
- [ ] PDB: retrieve an experimental structure, complete a verified CIF/PDB download, and demonstrate that a downstream analysis step can read the artifact and inspect its metadata.
- [ ] AlphaFold DB: retrieve a known available prediction by accession, verify a model download and available confidence metadata, and clearly identify it as predicted.
- [ ] Returned evidence and downloaded artifacts retain their source identifiers/URLs and retrieval metadata in subsequent analysis outputs.
- [ ] Automated tests cover domain result normalization and representative missing-record, malformed-input, rate-limit, and download-failure paths. Product-level validation covers connector selection, Inspector/Agent execution, and completed artifacts; mocked success alone is insufficient.
- [ ] User documentation describes supported operations, limitations, configuration, and reproducible examples for each source.

Implementation may be split into linked changes, but this feature remains open until the full five-database acceptance scope is verified.

issue:422.body:
## Problem
The `CodeCheck (GitCode)` check run on GitHub PRs only says "GitCode labelled the merge request `ci-failed`" and links to the GitCode MR. It doesn't name the failing rule or file. The GitCode MR page/API is not reachable for every contributor or reviewer (WAF/login). So authors end up writing "CodeCheck is ignored" (e.g. #421, also failing on #412 and #391), and reviewers can't tell whether a failure comes from the PR.

## Expected
When CodeCheck fails, the GitHub check-run output lists the failing checker/rule, file:line and message (or a stable public log link), so authors and reviewers can act without GitCode access.

## Verification cases
1. **Failure details mirrored**
   - Preconditions: a PR whose head introduces a known CodeCheck violation (e.g. a lint rule the GitCode pipeline enforces).
   - Steps: push; wait for the sync; open the `CodeCheck (GitCode)` check run on GitHub.
   - Expected / pass: `output.summary` or `output.text` names the rule, file:line and message; conclusion `failure`.
2. **Clean head**
   - Preconditions: a PR with no violations.
   - Steps: push; open the check run.
   - Expected / pass: conclusion `success`; no stale failure text from an earlier head.
3. **Infra failure isn't shown as a code failure (negative)**
   - Preconditions: the GitCode pipeline fails for an infra reason (timeout/sync error).
   - Steps: trigger; open the check run.
   - Expected / pass: output says it's an infra/sync failure, not a code violation, and links to a retry path.
4. **No secret leakage (security)**
   - Preconditions: a pipeline log that contains tokens/env.
   - Steps: mirror the failure details.
   - Expected / pass: mirrored text contains no tokens, cookies or internal URLs with credentials.

## Context
Refs #421, Refs #385. Seen at #421 head f494792 (GitCode MR !296) and #412 head 29e724a.

issue:423.body:
## Problem
In #421, the author reports that full `pnpm ci:ut` stops before test discovery: the local JiuwenSwarm checkout lacks the patch target files `agent_ws_server.py` and `call_timeout_patch.py`. The author says the same failure reproduces on detached upstream `main` (`a0cf9c77`). Contributors can't produce full-UT counts locally, so PRs fall back to focused suites only.

## Expected
`pnpm ci:ut` on a clean checkout of `main` (following the documented setup) reaches discovery and runs. Or, if the JiuwenSwarm patch targets moved, the setup fails with a clear message naming the expected JiuwenSwarm revision and how to get it.

## Verification cases
1. **Clean main runs full UT**
   - Preconditions: fresh clone of `main`, documented dev setup incl. JiuwenSwarm at the pinned revision.
   - Steps: `pnpm install`; `pnpm ci:ut`.
   - Expected / pass: discovery runs, a test count is reported, no "patch target missing" error.

   - Preconditions: JiuwenSwarm checked out at a revision without `agent_ws_server.py`/`call_timeout_patch.py`.
   - Steps: `pnpm ci:ut`.
   - Expected / pass: fails fast with a message naming the missing files and the required revision; exit code non-zero.
3. **CI parity**
   - Preconditions: GitHub `UT` job on the same commit.
   - Steps: compare the local `pnpm ci:ut` result with the CI UT job.
   - Expected / pass: same setup path and patch step; both pass or both fail for the same reason.

## Context
Refs #421, Refs #385. Reported in the #421 description (Validation section); not independently reproduced by the reviewer.

> Cross-tracking: [GitCode #96](https://gitcode.com/openJiuwen/sciencediscovery/issues/96) (Chinese counterpart of this issue).

## What I was trying to do

Drop a CSV into the workspace and preview it with the chart viewer (column names, missing values, distributions) before deciding what to ask.

## What I saw instead

Raw uploaded CSVs appear in the file list, but clicking one goes through `window.open` in a new tab (`openWorkspacePath` in `apps/web/src/App.tsx` hands every non-Markdown file to the browser), so it is shown as plain text or a download. The interactive table viewer — Plotly charts, filtering, column-type inference — is only available for files the agent formally declares as artifacts. The same file is a cold download link before asking, and a rich viewer after.

## Why this is confusing

Users cannot sanity-check their own data before sending it to the agent; the viewing experience of raw files and artifacts is split.

## Suggested user-observable outcome

Table files uploaded to the workspace open in the same interactive table viewer used for artifacts (charts, filtering, column-type inference), without waiting for an artifact declaration.

Design note: the viewer component already exists on the artifact path; this is mostly about wiring the workspace file path to it. Non-table files keep the current fallback. No API changes are expected — the existing workspace file-reading endpoint is reused.
